claims.text: The nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The nanoparticles are initially homogeneous solid solutions.
Differences in elemental surface energies drive surface segregation at elevated temperatures.
Bulk atomic diffusion governs phase stability in competition with surface segregation.
Trace-element or minor second-phase modification can increase atomic diffusion barriers.
Increasing diffusion barriers slows atomic migration.
Slower atomic migration mitigates segregation and helps preserve a uniform solid solution.
Bulk atomic diffusion counteracts surface segregation.
Temperature-dependent activation energies modulate the balance between surface segregation and bulk diffusion.
The balance between surface segregation and bulk diffusion governs structural and chemical stability.
Modified nanoparticles with enhanced diffusion barriers will exhibit less phase segregation than unmodified nanoparticles.
Modified nanoparticles will exhibit fewer compositional gradients than unmodified nanoparticles.
Modified nanoparticles will retain a more uniform crystal structure than unmodified nanoparticles throughout 473–1923 K.
The prediction is limited to controlled catalytic and thermoelectric environments in which temperature is the dominant variable.
External chemical reactions or other extreme conditions may introduce additional destabilizing mechanisms.
Equivalent segregation and compositional inhomogeneity in modified and unmodified samples would falsify the proposed benefit of enhanced diffusion barriers.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that bulk diffusion counteracts surface segregation, but also predicts that suppressing bulk atomic migration by increasing diffusion barriers will reduce segregation. Without distinguishing diffusion pathways or kinetic regimes, these causal directions conflict.
